'''Dan Shechtman''' ({{langx|he|דן שכטמן}}; born January 24, 1941)<ref name="oldcv">[http://www.academy.ac.il/data/persons_data/34/DshechtmanCV3.pdf Dan Shechtman] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111110224144/http://www.academy.ac.il/data/persons_data/34/DshechtmanCV3.pdf |date=November 10, 2011 }}. (PDF). Retrieved on January 28, 2012.</ref> is an Israeli chemist, the Philip Tobias Professor of Materials Science at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]], an Associate of the [[United States Department of Energy|US Department of Energy]]'s [[Ames National Laboratory]], and Professor of Materials Science at [[Iowa State University]]. On April 8, 1982, while on sabbatical at the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|U.S. National Bureau of Standards]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], Shechtman discovered the [[icosahedral phase]], which opened the new field of [[quasicrystal|quasiperiodic crystals]], also referred to as "[[Quasicrystal|quasicrystals]]."<ref name="discovery">{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=141067724 |title=Israeli Wins Chemistry Nobel For Quasicrystals |publisher=npr.org |access-date=October 5, 2011}}</ref> For this discovery, he was awarded the 2011 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], making him one of six Israelis who have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.<ref name="newswise1">[http://www.newswise.com/articles/iowa-state-ames-laboratory-technion-scientist-wins-nobel-prize-in-chemistry Iowa State, Ames Laboratory, Technion Scientist Wins Nobel Prize in Chemistry]. Newswise.com (October 5, 2011). Retrieved on January 28, 2012.</ref><ref>Multiple sources:
*[https://www.timesofisrael.com/tiny-israel-a-nobel-heavyweight-especially-in-chemistry/ Tiny Israel a Nobel heavyweight, especially in chemistry] ''[[Times of Israel]]''
*[http://english.alarabiya.net/articles/2011/10/06/170465.html Israel's Shechtman vindicated with Nobel for chemistry] AFP (in Al Arabiya News) Thursday, October 6, 2011
*{{cite web|last=Fiske |first=Gavriel |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/tiny-israel-a-nobel-heavyweight-especially-in-chemistry/ |title=Tiny Israel a Nobel heavyweight, especially in chemistry |publisher=Times of Israel |date=October 9, 2013 |access-date=October 13, 2013}}</ref>

==Biography==

=== Early life ===
Dan Shechtman was born in 1941 in [[Tel Aviv]], in what was then [[Mandatory Palestine]]; the city became part of the new state of [[Israel]] in 1948. He grew up in [[Petah Tikva]] and [[Ramat Gan]] in a [[Jews|Jewish]] family.<ref>{{Cite web |last=JINFO |title=Jewish Nobel Prize Winners in Chemistry |url=https://www.jinfo.org/Nobels_Chemistry.html |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=www.jinfo.org}}</ref> His grandparents had immigrated to Palestine during the  [[Second Aliyah]] (1904–1914) and founded a printing house. As a child, Shechtman was fascinated by [[Jules Verne]]'s ''[[The Mysterious Island]]'' (1874), which he read many times. His childhood dream was to become an engineer like the main protagonist, [[Cyrus Smith]].

{{blockquote|text=I thought that was the best thing a person could do. The engineer in the book knows mechanics and physics, and he creates a whole way of life on the island out of nothing. I wanted to be like that.|author=Dan Shechtman<ref name="Haaretz">{{cite web|url=https://www.haaretz.com/weekend/magazine/clear-as-crystal-1.353504|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110407085417/http://www.haaretz.com/weekend/magazine/clear-as-crystal-1.353504|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 7, 2011|title=Clear as crystal|publisher=Haaretz|date=April 1, 2011|access-date=October 6, 2011}}</ref>}}

=== Spouse and children ===
Shechtman is married to Prof. Tzipora Shechtman, Head of the Department of Counseling and Human Development at [[Haifa University]], and author of two books on [[psychotherapy]].<ref>[http://edu.haifa.ac.il/en/couns-ed/ Professor Zipora Shechtman] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120401192225/http://edu.haifa.ac.il/en/couns-ed/ |date=April 1, 2012 }}. Edu.haifa.ac.il. Retrieved on January 28, 2012.</ref><ref>[http://www.monstersandcritics.com/news/europe/news/article_1666890.php/He-deserves-it-wife-of-2011-Nobel-Chemistry-laureate-says He deserves it, wife of 2011 Nobel Chemistry laureate says] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111026232434/http://www.monstersandcritics.com/news/europe/news/article_1666890.php/He-deserves-it-wife-of-2011-Nobel-Chemistry-laureate-says |date=October 26, 2011 }}. Monstersandcritics.com (October 5, 2011). Retrieved on January 28, 2012.</ref> They have a son [[Yoav Shechtman]] (a former postdoctoral researcher in the lab of [[William E. Moerner|W. E. Moerner]] and now professor at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]]) and three daughters: Tamar Finkelstein (an organizational psychologist at the Israeli police leadership center), Ella Shechtman-Cory (a PhD in [[clinical psychology]]), and Ruth Dougoud-Nevo (also a PhD in clinical psychology).<ref>[http://mobile.bloomberg.com/news/2011-10-05/technion-s-shechtman-wins-chemistry-nobel-for-discovery-of-quasicrystals?category=%2Fnews%2Fmostread Shechtman Wins Chemistry Nobel for Crystal Find] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111218234522/http://mobile.bloomberg.com/news/2011-10-05/technion-s-shechtman-wins-chemistry-nobel-for-discovery-of-quasicrystals?category=%2Fnews%2Fmostread |date=December 18, 2011 }}. Mobile.bloomberg.com (October 5, 2011). Retrieved on January 28, 2012.</ref>

==Academic career==
[[File:Dan Shechtman in 1985.jpg|left|thumb|upright|Meeting at NIST in 1985 where Shechtman (left) explains the atomic structure of quasicrystals]]
After receiving his Ph.D. in [[Materials Engineering]] from the [[Technion]] in 1972, where he also obtained his B.Sc. in [[Mechanical Engineering]] in 1966 and M.Sc. in Materials Engineering in 1968,<ref name=oldcv /> Shechtman was an [[United States National Research Council|NRC]] fellow at the [[Air Force Research Laboratory|Aerospace Research Laboratories]] at [[Wright Patterson Air Force Base|Wright Patterson AFB]], Ohio, where he studied for three years the microstructure and physical [[metallurgy]] of [[titanium]] aluminides. In 1975, he joined the department of materials engineering at Technion. In 1981–1983 he was on sabbatical at [[Johns Hopkins University]], where he studied rapidly solidified [[aluminum]] transition metal alloys, in a joint program with [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NBS]]. During this study he discovered the [[icosahedral phase]] which opened the new field of [[Quasicrystal|quasiperiodic crystals]].

In 1992–1994 he was on sabbatical at [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST), where he studied the effect of the defect structure of [[Chemical vapor deposition of diamond|CVD diamond]] on its growth and properties. Shechtman's Technion research is conducted in the Louis Edelstein Center, and in the Wolfson Centre which is headed by him. He served on several Technion Senate Committees and headed one of them.

Shechtman joined the Iowa State faculty in 2004. He currently spends about five months a year in [[Ames, Iowa|Ames]] on a part-time appointment.<ref name="newswise1"/><ref>[http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/breaking/chi-iowa-state-prof-wins-nobel-in-chemistry-20111005,0,6056569.story Iowa State prof wins Nobel in chemistry] ([[Chicago Tribune]], October 5, 2011)</ref>

Since 2014 he has been the head of the International Scientific Council of [[Tomsk Polytechnic University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://news.tpu.ru/news/2014/04/04/21422-inter-union.html |title=В ТПУ впервые прошло заседание Международного научного совета |access-date=September 1, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903100623/http://news.tpu.ru/news/2014/04/04/21422-inter-union.html |archive-date=September 3, 2014 }}</ref>

==Work on quasicrystals and controversy==
[[File:Quasicrystal1.jpg|thumb|Shechtman's Nobel Prize–winning work was in the area of [[quasicrystal]]s, ordered crystalline materials lacking repeating structures, such as this Al-Pd-Mn alloy.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ünal|first=B |author2=V. Fournée |author3=K.J. Schnitzenbaumer |author4=C. Ghosh |author5=C.J. Jenks |author5-link=Cynthia Jenks|author6=A.R. Ross |author7=T.A. Lograsso |author8=J.W. Evans |author9=P.A. Thiel|title=Nucleation and growth of Ag islands on fivefold Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystal surfaces: Dependence of island density on temperature and flux|journal=Physical Review B|year=2007|volume=75|article-number=064205|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.75.064205|bibcode = 2007PhRvB..75f4205U|issue=6 |s2cid=53382207 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01665118/file/Baris-REA.pdf }}</ref>]]
[[File:Nobel Dan Shechtman 2011-12-08.ogv|thumb|Interview with Dan Shechtman after his Nobel lecture]]
A [[quasiperiodic]] [[crystal]], or, in short, [[quasicrystal]], is a [[structure]] that is [[Order and disorder (physics)|ordered]] but not [[Bravais lattice|periodic]]. A quasicrystalline pattern can continuously fill all available space, but it lacks [[translational symmetry]].<ref name="janot1997">
{{cite book |last=Janot |first=Christian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dpPePU-xs2oC |title=Quasicrystals – a primer, 2nd ed. |publisher=Oxford University Publishing |year=1997 |isbn=0-19-856551-8}}</ref> "[[Aperiodic mosaic]]s, such as those found in the medieval Islamic mosaics of the [[Alhambra palace]] in [[Spain]] and the [[Darb-e Imam|Darb-i Imam shrine]] in [[Iran]], have helped scientists understand what quasicrystals look like at the atomic level. In those mosaics, as in quasicrystals, the patterns are regular – they follow mathematical rules – but they never repeat themselves."<ref name="reuters20111005" />

The Nobel Committee at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said that "his discovery was extremely controversial," but that his work "eventually forced scientists to reconsider their conception of the very nature of matter."<ref name="reuters20111005" /> Through Shechtman's discovery, several other groups were able to form similar quasicrystals by 1987, finding these materials to have low [[Thermal conductivity and resistivity|thermal]] and [[Electrical resistivity and conductivity|electrical]] conductivity, while possessing high structural stability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Day |first=Charles |date=February 1, 2001 |title=Binary Quasicrystals Discovered That Are Stable and Icosahedral |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1359699 |journal=Physics Today |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=17–18 |bibcode=2001PhT....54b..17D |doi=10.1063/1.1359699 |issn=0031-9228}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=N. |last2=Chen |first2=H. |last3=Kuo |first3=K. H. |date=August 31, 1987 |title=Two-dimensional quasicrystal with eightfold rotational symmetry |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.1010 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=59 |issue=9 |pages=1010–1013 |bibcode=1987PhRvL..59.1010W |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.1010 |pmid=10035936 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bancel |first1=Peter A. |last2=Heiney |first2=Paul A. |date=June 15, 1986 |title=Icosahedral aluminum--transition-metal alloys |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.33.7917 |journal=Physical Review B |volume=33 |issue=12 |pages=7917–7922 |bibcode=1986PhRvB..33.7917B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.33.7917 |pmid=9938181 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Quasicrystals have also been found naturally.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crane |first=Leah |date=December 8, 2016 |title=Third-ever natural quasicrystal found in Siberian meteorite |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2115570-third-ever-natural-quasicrystal-found-in-siberian-meteorite/ |access-date=January 28, 2022 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bindi |first1=Luca |last2=Eiler |first2=John M. |last3=Guan |first3=Yunbin |last4=Hollister |first4=Lincoln S. |last5=MacPherson |first5=Glenn |last6=Steinhardt |first6=Paul J. |last7=Yao |first7=Nan |date=January 31, 2012 |title=Evidence for the extraterrestrial origin of a natural quasicrystal |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=109 |issue=5 |pages=1396–1401 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1111115109 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=3277151 |pmid=22215583 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

From the day Shechtman published his findings on quasicrystals in 1984 to the day [[Linus Pauling]] died in 1994, Shechtman experienced hostility from Pauling toward the non-periodic interpretation. "For a long time it was me against the world," Shechtman said. "I was a subject of ridicule and lectures about the basics of [[crystallography]]. The leader of the opposition to my findings was the two-time Nobel Laureate Linus Pauling, the idol of the [[American Chemical Society]] and one of the most famous scientists in the world. For years, 'til his last day, he fought against quasi-periodicity in crystals. He was wrong, and after a while, I enjoyed every moment of this scientific battle, knowing that he was wrong."<ref>{{cite press release |title=Iowa State, Ames Laboratory, Technion scientist wins Nobel Prize in Chemistry |url=https://www.news.iastate.edu/news/2011/oct/dannynobel |publisher=Iowa State University |location=Ames, Iowa |date=October 5, 2011 |access-date=January 16, 2019 |archive-date=May 25, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230525163631/https://www.news.iastate.edu/news/2011/oct/dannynobel }}</ref> Pauling is noted saying "There is no such thing as quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists."<ref name="reuters20111005">
{{cite news |last=Lannin |first=Patrick |date=October 5, 2011 |title=Ridiculed crystal work wins Nobel for Israeli |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/nobel-chemistry-idUSL5E7L51U620111005 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230526075257/https://www.reuters.com/article/nobel-chemistry-idUSL5E7L51U620111005 |archive-date=May 26, 2023 |access-date=October 22, 2011 |newspaper=Reuters}}</ref> Pauling was apparently unaware of a paper in 1981 by [[Hagen Kleinert|H. Kleinert]] and K. Maki which had pointed out the possibility of a non-periodic [[Icosahedral Phase]] in [[quasicrystal]]s<ref>{{cite journal | title = Lattice Textures in Cholesteric Liquid Crystals | author = Kleinert H., Maki K. | journal = Fortschritte der Physik | volume = 29 | issue = 5 | pages = 219–259 | year = 1981 | doi = 10.1002/prop.19810290503 | url = https://hagenkleinert.de/documents/articles/75.pdf|bibcode = 1981ForPh..29..219K }}</ref> (see the
[https://web.archive.org/web/20230213224502/http://users.physik.fu-berlin.de/~kleinert/icosahedral/index.html historical notes]). The head of Shechtman's research group told him to "go back and read the textbook" and a couple of days later "asked him to leave for 'bringing disgrace' on the team."<ref>
{{cite news|first=Alok |last=Jha|title=Dan Shechtman: 'Linus Pauling said I was talking nonsense' |newspaper=Guardian|date=January 5, 2013|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2013/jan/06/dan-shechtman-nobel-prize-chemistry-interview}}
</ref> Shechtman felt rejected.<ref name="reuters20111005" /> On publication of his paper, other scientists began to confirm and accept empirical findings of the existence of quasicrystals.<ref name="SB-DB-100511">{{cite web |last=Bradley |first=David |title=Dan Shechtman discusses quasicrystals |url=http://www.sciencebase.com/science-blog/dan-shechtman-discusses-quasicrystals-nobelprize.html |publisher=ScienceBase |access-date=October 5, 2011 |date=October 5, 2011}} Shechtman video interview</ref><ref>
{{cite web |url=https://www.haaretz.com/weekend/magazine/clear-as-crystal-1.353504 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110407085417/http://www.haaretz.com/weekend/magazine/clear-as-crystal-1.353504 |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 7, 2011 |title=Clear as crystal |publisher=Haaretz |date=April 1, 2011 |access-date=October 6, 2011}}</ref>

Quasicrystalline materials could be{{update after|2014|6|10}}<!-- what applications of this theoretical work have come now, years after the theoretical findings, and even several years after the Nobel prize to Shectman --> used in a large number of applications, including the formation of durable steel used for fine instrumentation, and non-stick insulation for electrical wires and cooking equipment.,<ref name="nature nobel">
{{cite journal | url = http://www.nature.com/news/2011/111005/full/news.2011.572.html |title = Impossible crystals snag chemistry Nobel | first= Richard | last = Van Noorden | date = October 5, 2011 | access-date = October 5, 2011 |journal = [[nature (journal)|nature]]|doi = 10.1038/news.2011.572 | url-access = subscription }}</ref><ref name="bbc nobel">
{{cite web | url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-15181187 |title = Nobel win for crystal discovery | first= Jennifer | last = Carpenter | date = October 5, 2011 | access-date = October 5, 2011 | publisher = BBC}}</ref> but presently have no technological applications.

The Nobel prize was 10 million [[Swedish krona]] (approximately {{USD|1.5 million}}).<ref name="reuters20111005" />

==Presidential bid==
[[File:Reuven Rivlin hosted the winners declaration event of the 2018 Wolf Prize, February 2018 (6355).jpg|thumb|Shechtman and President [[Reuven Rivlin]], present the [[Wolf Prize]] award in 2018. Behind them is an [[Visual arts in Israel|Israeli basalt ash relief]].]]
On January 17, 2014, in an interview with Israel's [[Channel 1 (Israel)|Channel One]], Shechtman announced his candidacy for [[President of Israel]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.jpost.com/National-News/Nobel-Prize-winning-professor-announces-run-for-President-of-Israel-338551 | title=Nobel Prize winning professor announces run for president of Israel| date=January 17, 2014}}</ref> Shechtman received the endorsement of the ten Members of [[Knesset]] required to run. In the [[2014 Israeli presidential election|elections]], held on June 10, 2014, he was awarded only one vote. This led Israeli press and Israeli humorists to qualify Shechtman as "quasi-president" in reference to the "quasi-scientist" quote.
